These exit figures are the fictional protagonist's own in-story scouting numbers (Four's calculations), not a real-world claim, and are not treated as needing external sourcing -- consistent with how the original source itself presents them (Four literally 'has calculated' these numbers as a character skill, not a cited statistic). The original's Appendix C risk-factor table (per-mile road-type risk, stoplight/stop-sign increments, the y=1.42^x speeding formula, per-minute-in-vehicle risk, police-station-proximity bumps) is reused verbatim as the numeric content of case.md's Appendix C, reframed explicitly as Four's own disclosed Modeling Assumptions rather than presented as sourced fact, since no public dataset of 'odds of capture per stoplight' exists -- this is a genuine NOT FOUND->Modeling Assumption outcome, not an invention. What the original case lacked entirely: (1) a real, drivable route -- the original's Appendix A/B were screenshot-only Boise/police maps embedded as images in the source docx, not machine-readable, and the actual destination ('Heroes Academy,' named literally in the original Challenge text) was never geolocated. (2) a sensitivity model and disclosed margin -- neither existed in the original. (3) FACILITATOR.md's 11-anchor ladder, timed Socratic plan, and cohort bands -- the original Guide Notes have a shorter 5-anchor structure (Intro/Anchor1/Anchor2/Anchor3/Anchor5 -- Anchor 4 is literally missing/skipped a number in the source itself) with no timing and no cohort-size guidance; this conversion reformats to the current 11-anchor doctrine while preserving every real beat from the source (the meter-maid/stolen-vehicle Twist, the 5 Close questions, the Monday Case Study Launch content) as FACILITATOR.md content, none of it invented. A structural property worth flagging explicitly rather than hiding: because both exit options share the identical getaway route, drive, and risk factors, every stated Modeling Assumption in Appendix C (road-type mix, stoplight/stop-sign counts, per-minute risk) applies identically to A and B and mathematically cancels out of the A-vs-B comparison -- the margin between the two options is set entirely by the two given, locked exit numbers (94% vs. 98%), and is structurally invariant to every route assumption. This is disclosed in FACILITATOR.md and sensitivity_note below, not discovered only at QA time.

balance.argument_a: The street-level exit's 94% figure already prices in real slack: 17 of the allotted 30 seconds, leaving 13 full seconds (43% of the window) of cushion for anything that doesn't go exactly to plan -- a dropped bag, a jammed door, one extra pedestrian to dodge. A crew that values margin for error over the raw headline percentage has a real, quantifiable reason to prefer A.
balance.argument_b: The underground garage's 98% is the higher number on every metric that is actually being graded -- both the building-exit chance itself and, once multiplied through the identical shared getaway drive, the final combined probability of a clean escape (74.91% vs. 71.85%, a real 3.06-percentage-point gap). Every stated route assumption in Appendix C applies equally to both options and cancels out of the comparison, so this gap is not fragile to any of them -- it is set entirely by the two given exit numbers, which already are Four's own considered odds.
balance.margin_basis: Route survival probability (shared by both options): P = (1-0.0029)^2.0 x (1-0.012)^6.4 x (1-0.0008)^0.5 x (1-0.0165)^7 x (1-0.004)^3 x (1-0.0027)^21 = 0.76434 (Appendix A/C). Option A total = 0.94 x 0.76434 = 0.71848 (71.85%). Option B total = 0.98 x 0.76434 = 0.74906 (74.91%). Margin = (74.91 - 71.85) / 71.85 = 4.26%, Option B (underground garage) wins on the graded primary metric. The 30-second-window buffer argument for A (13s vs. 1s of slack) is real, disclosed context for discussion, not the graded primary metric.

modeling_assumptions.text: The real 8.9-mile route (Appendix A, S3) is segmented into 2.0 mi city road / 6.4 mi state highway / 0.5 mi neighborhood road, matching the real named roads (downtown Boise streets, then W Chinden Blvd / US-20 W / US-26 W, a real U.S. highway) to Appendix C's risk categories, since Google's routing tool reports one combined distance rather than a category-by-category split.

Stoplight and stop sign counts along the route (7 stoplights, 3 stop signs) are fixed by this case as a plausible count for a mixed downtown-plus-highway 8.9-mile Boise route -- no public database counts traffic control devices along an arbitrary route.

All of Appendix C's per-mile, per-stoplight, per-stop-sign, per-minute, and per-station-proximity risk percentages are Four's own disclosed professional judgment, reused verbatim from the original 2021 case source, not drawn from any public crime-rate dataset (none exists at this granularity).

The crew obeys posted speed limits by default; Appendix C's speeding formula (y = 1.42^x) is real appendix data but is not required by any Challenge deliverable, consistent with T3's deliberate inclusion of data a Hero may choose to use or ignore.

sensitivity_note: Structural finding, disclosed rather than left for a guide to discover live: because Option A and Option B share the identical getaway route, every stated route assumption in Appendix C (road-type mix, stoplight/stop-sign counts, per-minute-in-vehicle rate) enters both options' final percentage identically and cancels out of the margin -- flexing any of them, in either direction, changes both options' final percentages by the same multiplicative factor and therefore never changes the 4.26% margin or the winner (verified via sensitivity_model.py's FLEX sweep, case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5). The only two numbers that can move the margin or flip the winner are the two given, locked exit figures themselves (94%/98%), which are the case's fixed dilemma parameters, not modeling assumptions open to a ±50% flex. This is a real, load-bearing property of the case's math -- a Hero who spends all their effort trying to build two different route-risk models for A and B (rather than recognizing the shared route cancels out) is falling into the case's actual trap; see FACILITATOR.md.
